entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Vātsyāyana, a foundational figure in classical Indian philosophy and erotology, flourished likely in the 3rd century CE, possibly within the intellectual milieu of Pataliputra, the capital of the Gupta or pre-Gupta Magadha. His enduring significance stems from his authorship of the *Kāma Sūtra*, a Sanskrit treatise that transcends its popular reputation as a mere sex manual to offer a comprehensive sociological and psychological guide to artha (material prosperity) and kama (pleasure), two of the four purusharthas (aims of human life) in ancient Hindu philosophy. He synthesized and systematized earlier traditions of *kama-shastra*, providing an unparalleled window into the domestic, social, and aesthetic norms of elite urban society in ancient India.

Composed during a period of significant cultural and intellectual efflorescence in India, the *Kāma Sūtra* is structured into seven parts, covering topics from the acquisition of knowledge and the pursuit of pleasure, to the arts of seduction, marriage, and the conduct of courtesans. While Vātsyāyana himself remains an enigmatic figure, possibly a *brahmacharin* (celibate student) or an ascetic, his work meticulously details the sophisticated urban lifestyle (*nāgaraka*) and its pursuit of refined pleasures (*kāma*) as an integral part of a balanced life, alongside dharma (righteous conduct) and artha. The text draws upon, and often critiques, preceding texts and schools of thought, consolidating a vast body of knowledge on human relationships, social etiquette, and aesthetic appreciation.

entities.summary:
Vātsyāyana, an ancient Indian philosopher and scholar, is primarily known as the purported author of the *Kama Sutra*, a foundational Sanskrit treatise on human sexual behavior, social etiquette, and the art of living. Though his exact dates and biography remain shrouded in scholarly debate, he is generally placed in the Gupta period, likely between the 2nd and 4th centuries CE, a golden age of Indian intellectual and artistic flourishing. His work provides an invaluable window into the social structures, daily life, and ethical considerations of classical Indian society, transcending its popular association with mere sexual instruction to offer a comprehensive guide to *kama*, one of the four purusharthas (aims of human life) in Hinduism, alongside *dharma* (righteous conduct), *artha* (economic prosperity), and *moksha* (spiritual liberation).

The *Kama Sutra*, far from being solely a sex manual, is a sophisticated text of *kāmashastra* (science of desire) that systematizes various aspects of urban life, courtship, marriage, and family dynamics. It meticulously details practices ranging from personal hygiene and social graces to the responsibilities of a householder and the nuances of erotic pleasure. Vātsyāyana synthesized existing traditions and oral knowledge into a structured, didactic work, often citing earlier authorities. His methodology reflects a detached, almost scientific approach to human relationships and desires, categorizing and analyzing behaviors with remarkable precision and advocating for a balanced pursuit of pleasure within a moral and social framework.
